title: Shortest Cut to a Divisible Total
statement:
You get an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer p. Remove one contiguous block of elements (it may be empty) so that the sum of what remains is divisible by p.

Return the length of the shortest block that works. You are not allowed to remove the whole array. If no block works, return -1.

examples.why: The total is 18, which leaves 4 over a multiple of 7. No single element has remainder 4, but 8 + 3 = 11 does. Removing [8, 3] leaves 7.
The total 9 leaves remainder 1. Only the whole array has that remainder, and removing everything is not allowed.
Total 11, remainder 2. Neither 1 nor 4 alone has remainder 2, but the block [1, 4] sums to 5, which does.

hints: Let rem = total % p. Which blocks are you looking for, in terms of their own sum?
You need a block whose sum leaves the same remainder rem. With prefix sums, block (i, j] has sum pre[j] − pre[i], so you need pre[i] ≡ pre[j] − rem (mod p).
Scan j from left to right and keep a map from each prefix remainder to the latest index where it appeared. The latest one gives the shortest block ending at j.

explain.intuition:
If the total leaves remainder rem, the block you remove must leave exactly that same remainder; then the rest is a multiple of p. If rem is 0, remove nothing.

Block sums are differences of prefix sums, and remainders subtract the same way: block (i, j] works when pre[i] mod p equals (pre[j] − rem) mod p. This is the familiar "two-sum on prefix sums" trick. For each j you want the matching i as close as possible, so store the latest index for each prefix remainder. The only special rule: a block covering the whole array does not count.
steps: Compute rem = total % p. If it is 0, return 0.
Put remainder 0 at index −1 in a map (the empty prefix).
Scan left to right, keeping cur = prefix % p. Look up (cur − rem + p) % p; if found at index i, the block length is j − i.
If the best length equals n (or nothing was found), return −1.
pitfalls: Accepting the whole array as the block. [3, 3, 3] with p = 4 must return −1.
Storing the first index of each remainder instead of the latest. That finds the longest block, not the shortest.
Letting the prefix sum grow unbounded. In languages with fixed-size integers it overflows; keep it reduced mod p.

solutions.title: Try every block
solutions.idea: For each start, extend the block to the right and track its sum mod p. Keep the shortest block whose remainder equals the total's.

solutions.title: Prefix remainders in a hash map
solutions.idea: A block works when its prefix remainders differ by rem. Keep the latest index of each prefix remainder to get the shortest block ending at each position.

followups: Remove a block so that the remaining sum is divisible by p and is as large as possible. What changes?
Instead of one block, you may remove any subsequence. How would you find the fewest elements to remove?
